lines.text: Monday morning. Four agents are working in four terminals, on four projects.
One finished an hour ago. One has waited forty minutes for your yes. One is stuck. You find out only by checking every window.
Agent R Q puts every agent on one screen: what it is on, who it is waiting for, where the time went, and every command it asked to run.
A terminal tells you nothing until you go and look. And while you look at one, the other three keep going.
Here, the workspaces page comes first. Each card names the agent working in it, with a green dot while it is connected.
Its chips count the work: ongoing, to do, and, in yellow, the actions waiting on you.
Switch to Detailed, and each card lists its open tasks, the one in progress first.
The Kanban board puts every workspace's tasks on one board: Not Started, Ongoing, Blocked and Done.
Each card shows its workspace and the agent that moved it last. Click it, and you are in its thread.
Nothing needs a refresh. When billing's agent finishes the VAT export, its card moves to Done, and a toast tells you so.
An agent asked for a yes forty minutes ago. You were in another window, and it has waited ever since.
Here, the billing agent wants to run the migration that adds a tax rate column. The request comes to you, with the tool and the exact command.
A toast says permission required, billing's card shows an action chip, and Pending on Me lists the request.
Allow it once, always allow it, or deny it. Allow and Deny are on its board card too, so you don't even have to open it.
The docs agent needs a decision: keep the old API in the guide, or only the new one? So it marks its task blocked. The card moves to the red column, and the sidebar shows docs is blocked.
You answer in its thread, only the new one, and the agent picks up where it stopped.
Is it still working, or is it stuck? A quiet terminal looks the same either way.
Open a task, and you see it: the agent is working, for how long, and the last three tools it used.
Type while it works, and your message reaches it at once, in the middle of its work. No restart, no new prompt.
Each agent works on one task at a time. The rest wait in Not Started, and the agent takes them in the order you set.
Two hours on one task. How much was work, and how much was waiting for you?
Every task keeps a timeline. Each change of status adds a dot, with the time spent written on the line to the next one.
Red is time blocked. Yellow is time waiting for your answer. The current dot pulses, and its clock keeps running.
The totals add it up: time worked, time blocked, time waiting on you, and start to close.
This refunds task ran two hours start to close. An hour and fourteen minutes was work, thirty-eight minutes blocked, and eight minutes waiting on your yes.
Something changed in the repo overnight. Which agent ran what, and who said yes?
Switch the task to Trajectory. Its badge counts the tool calls, and the lanes show the shape of the whole run.
Search for migrate, or keep a single lane, to find one moment in a long run.
Click a call to see the tool, whether it was allowed, auto-allowed or denied, and the exact command it sent.
Here is the one you said no to: a force push to main, denied in red, then the plain push that followed, allowed.
But seeing everything should not mean approving everything.
Always allow saves a rule to the workspace, such as npm with any arguments. The next npm call is auto-allowed, and the trajectory says so.
Every rule is listed in the workspace settings, and one click removes it.
And the board is yours too. Drag a card to change its status, or move it up so it goes first.
Every agent on one screen, the requests waiting on you, what each one is doing now, where the time went, and every call on the record.
What do you check first when an agent goes quiet? Tell us in the comments, and try it at Agent R Q dot com.
